body: Of 28 windows in this library, 14 have their best starting point within about nine months of the Mar 2009 low (Bajaj Finance, Astral, Pidilite, Titan, Eicher, Balkrishna, APL Apollo, Deepak, Tata Elxsi, Avanti, Caplin, La Opala, Alkyl, Symphony). Another nine start within about six months of the Mar 2020 COVID low (KPIT, Trent, Cochin, Mazagon, HAL, BEL, BSE, Suzlon, and CDSL near it). Only Page (2007 IPO), Garware (2013), Polycab/Dixon (2019 IPO/low) and Kaynes (2022 IPO) start elsewhere. Two implications. (1) The headline multiples (100–2,000x) are partly a start-point artefact; buying the same names a year before or after the crash gives 2–5x less. (2) The real edge was owning or buying quality growers when they were at 5–15x during a panic; in 2008–09 and 2020 many of these traded at single-digit P/E. Process: keep a ready list of high-ROCE, low-debt compounders with pre-set 'crash prices' so a crash is an execution step, not a decision. Survival (no leverage, cash reserve) is what makes this possible. Link: insight:avoid-ruin.
title: ~23 of 28 Indian multibagger windows start within months of the Mar 2009 or Mar 2020 lows

body: Ritter Table 16e (9,195 operating-company IPOs 1975-2021, 3-year buy-and-hold from first close): BHR below -50%: 38.5%; -50% to 0%: 21.5%; 0-50%: 14.5%; 50-100%: 9.5%; 100-200%: 8.3%; 200-500%: 6.0%; 500-1,000%: 1.3%; above 1,000% (11x+): 0.5% (39 of 9,195). Mean 38.1% but median 2.6% - the mean is carried by a thin right tail, the same skew Bessembinder found for all stocks. For IPOs with LTM sales >= $100m (2025$; 4,112 IPOs) the left tail shrinks: 25.9% lose more than half (vs 38.5%), and 51.2% are positive. Lesson for a multibagger hunter: the 10x IPO exists but is ~1-in-200 over 3 years; a basket of small IPOs loses to the market. Requiring real revenue (>= $100m) cuts the wipe-out rate by about a third. Base rate to quote before any IPO enthusiasm.
title: US IPO 3-year return distribution: 60% lose money, 38.5% lose over half, 0.5% go 10x+

body: Kahneman and Tversky, 'On the Psychology of Prediction' (Psychological Review 80(4), 1973; ~3,900 Crossref citations). In the 'Tom W.' and engineer/lawyer experiments, people predicted almost entirely from how representative a description seemed and largely ignored prior probabilities. Told a sample was 70% lawyers or 30% lawyers, subjects gave nearly the same answers for a stereotype-matching description. They also made predictions that were not regressive enough: extreme inputs produced extreme forecasts even when the inputs were unreliable. Lovallo and Kahneman, 'Delusions of Success: How Optimism Undermines Executives' Decisions' (Harvard Business Review, July 2003; ~700 citations): executives plan from the 'inside view' (the details of this project) and so routinely overestimate benefits and underestimate costs and time. The remedy is 'reference class forecasting': pick a class of similar past cases, take its outcome distribution, and adjust modestly. Flyvbjerg's megaproject data (9 in 10 over budget) are the large-scale replication. Replicated: base-rate neglect is among the most replicated findings in judgment research, though it weakens when base rates are presented as frequencies (Gigerenzer). Use for us: this is why memdb stores base rates. For each thesis, first retrieve the reference class from the knowledge base: Indian IPOs (40-50% below issue), turnarounds, capex-heavy cyclicals, multibagger starting P/E, small-cap drawdown durations, the 4% of stocks that create all wealth. Then adjust only with specific, verified evidence, and regress a company's recent extreme growth toward the class mean.

data.kt1973: predictions follow representativeness, ignore priors, insufficiently regressive

title: Base-rate neglect (Kahneman-Tversky 1973) and the outside view (Lovallo-Kahneman 2003): start every estimate from a reference class
